Well-posedness of the Green-Naghdi and Boussinesq-Peregrine systems

Vincent Duchêne ††thanks: IRMAR - UMR6625, CNRS and Univ. Rennes 1, Campus de Beaulieu, F-35042 Rennes cedex, France. VD is partially supported by the project Dyficolti ANR-13-BS01-0003-01 of the Agence Nationale de la Recherche.    Samer Israwi ††thanks: Mathématiques, Faculté des sciences I et Ecole doctorale des sciences et technologie, Université Libanaise, Beyrouth, Liban. SI is partially supported by the Lebanese University research program (MAA group project).
August 24, 2026
Abstract

In this paper we address the Cauchy problem for two systems modeling the propagation of long gravity waves in a layer of homogeneous, incompressible and inviscid fluid delimited above by a free surface, and below by a non-necessarily flat rigid bottom. Concerning the Green-Naghdi system, we improve the result of Alvarez-Samaniego and Lannes [5] in the sense that much less regular data are allowed, and no loss of derivatives is involved. Concerning the Boussinesq-Peregrine system, we improve the lower bound on the time of existence provided by Mésognon-Gireau [42]. The main ingredient is a physically motivated change of unknowns revealing the quasilinear structure of the systems, from which energy methods are implemented.

1 Introduction

1.1 Motivation

The Green-Naghdi system11 1 The Boussinesq-Peregrine system can be viewed as a simplification of the Green-Naghdi system for small-amplitude waves, which is particularly relevant for numerical purposes; see [45, 31, 42, 7]. This work is dedicated to the Green-Naghdi system and we only remark incidentally that our strategy may also be favorably applied to the Boussinesq-Peregrine system. (sometimes called Serre or fully nonlinear Boussinesq system) is a model for the propagation of gravity waves in a layer of homogeneous incompressible inviscid fluid with rigid bottom and free surface. It has been formally derived several times in the literature, in particular in [48, 51, 24, 39, 47], using different techniques and various hypotheses. For a clear and modern exposition, it is shown in [32] that the Green-Naghdi system can be derived as an asymptotic model from the water waves system (namely the “exact” equations for the propagation of surface gravity waves), by assuming that the typical horizontal length of the flow is much larger than the depth of the fluid layer —that is in the shallow-water regime— and that the flow is irrotational. Roughly speaking, a Taylor expansion with respect to the small “shallow-water parameter” yields at first order the Saint-Venant system, and at second order the Green-Naghdi system (see for instance [38] for higher order systems). As a relatively simple fully nonlinear model (that is without restriction on the amplitude of the waves) formally improving the precision of the Saint-Venant system, the Green-Naghdi system is widely used to model and numerically simulate the propagation of surface waves, in particular in coastal oceanography. It would be impossible to review the vast literature on the subject, and we only let the reader refer to [6, 10] for an introduction and relevant references.

In this work, we are interested in the structural properties and rigorous justification of the Green-Naghdi system. The derivation through formal Taylor expansions of Bonneton and Lannes [32] can be made rigorous [31, Prop. 5.8]: roughly speaking, any sufficiently smooth solution of the water waves system satisfies the Green-Naghdi system up to a quantifiable (small) remainder. This consistency result is only one step towards the full justification of the model in the following sense: the solution of the water waves system and the solution of the Green-Naghdi system with corresponding initial data remain close on a relevant time interval. In order for such result to hold, one needs of course to ensure the existence and uniqueness of a solution to the Green-Naghdi system in the aforementioned time interval for a large class of initial data; one also needs a stability property ensuring that the two solutions are close. These two results typically call for robust energy estimates on exact and approximate solutions.

Somewhat surprisingly, the well-posedness theory concerning the Cauchy problem for the Green-Naghdi system is in some sense less satisfactory than the corresponding one for the water waves system. Again, the literature on the latter problem is too vast to summarize, and we only mention the result of [4, 26] and [31, Theorem 4.16]. Indeed, the latter pay attention to the various dimensionless parameters of the system, and in particular obtain results which hold uniformly with respect to the shallow-water parameter. The outcome of these results is that provided that the initial data is sufficiently regular (measured through Sobolev spaces) and satisfy physical assumptions —the so-called non-cavitation and Rayleigh-Taylor criteria— then there exists a unique solution of the water waves system preserving the regularity of the initial data. Moreover, the maximal time of existence may be bounded from below uniformly with respect to the shallow-water parameter; see details therein. Such result is very much nontrivial as the limit of small shallow-water parameter is singular in some sense. Similar results have been proved for the Green-Naghdi system in horizontal dimension d=1d=1 in [37] (for flat bottom) and [28] (for general bathymetries), but are not yet available in dimension d=2d=2. Alvarez-Samaniego and Lannes [5] proved an existence and uniqueness result on the correct time-scale but their proof relies on a Nash-Moser scheme, and as such involves a loss of derivatives between the regularity of the initial data and the control of the solution at positive times. The main result of this paper is to show that this loss of derivatives is in fact not necessary, and that the Cauchy problem for the Green-Naghdi system is well-posed in the sense of Hadamard in Sobolev-type spaces.

1.2 Strategy

Let us now introduce the system of equations at stake. In order to ease the discussion and notations, we restrict the study to the horizontal space X∈ℝdX\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with d=2d=2, although the results are easily adapted to the situation of d=1d=1, thus yielding another proof of the result in [28]. The non-dimensionalized Green-Naghdi system may be expressed (see [32, 31]) as

(1.1) {∂tζ+∇⋅(h​𝐮)=0,(Id+μ𝒯[h,βb])∂t𝐮+∇ζ+ϵ(𝐮⋅∇)𝐮+μϵ(𝒬[h,𝐮]+𝒬b[h,βb,𝐮])=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta+\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u})=0,\\ \\ \big({\rm Id}+\mu\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]\big)\partial_{t}{\bf u}+\nabla\zeta+\epsilon({\bf u}\cdot\nabla){\bf u}+\mu\epsilon\big(\mathcal{Q}[h,{\bf u}]+\mathcal{Q}_{b}[h,\beta b,{\bf u}]\big)=0,\end{array}\right.

with h=1+ϵ​ζ−β​bh=1+\epsilon\zeta-\beta b and

(1.2) 𝒯⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮\displaystyle\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u} =def−13​h∇(h3∇⋅𝐮)+12​h(∇(h2(β∇b)⋅𝐮)−h2(β∇b)∇⋅𝐮)+β2(∇b⋅𝐮)∇b,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{-1}{3h}\nabla(h^{3}\nabla\cdot{\bf u})+\frac{1}{2h}\Big(\nabla\big(h^{2}(\beta\nabla b)\cdot{\bf u}\big)-h^{2}(\beta\nabla b)\nabla\cdot{\bf u}\Big)+\beta^{2}(\nabla b\cdot{\bf u})\nabla b,
𝒬⁡[h,𝐮]\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}[h,{\bf u}] =def−13​h∇(h3((𝐮⋅∇)(∇⋅𝐮)−(∇⋅𝐮)2)),\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{-1}{3h}\nabla\Big(h^{3}\big(({\bf u}\cdot\nabla)(\nabla\cdot{\bf u})-(\nabla\cdot{\bf u})^{2}\big)\Big),
𝒬b​[h,β​b,𝐮]\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{b}[h,\beta b,{\bf u}] =defβ2​h(∇(h2(𝐮⋅∇)2b)−h2((𝐮⋅∇)(∇⋅𝐮)−(∇⋅𝐮)2)∇b)+β2((𝐮⋅∇)2b)∇b.\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{\beta}{2h}\Big(\nabla\big(h^{2}({\bf u}\cdot\nabla)^{2}b\big)-h^{2}\big(({\bf u}\cdot\nabla)(\nabla\cdot{\bf u})-(\nabla\cdot{\bf u})^{2}\big)\nabla b\Big)+\beta^{2}\big(({\bf u}\cdot\nabla)^{2}b\big)\nabla b.

Here, the unknowns are ζ⁡(t,X)∈ℝ\zeta(t,X)\in\mathbb{R} and 𝐮⁡(t,X)∈ℝd{\bf u}(t,X)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (representing respectively the dimensionless surface deformation and layer-averaged horizontal velocity), b⁡(X)∈ℝb(X)\in\mathbb{R} is the fixed bottom topography (so that h⁡(t,X)h(t,X) represents the depth of the fluid layer) and ϵ,β,μ\epsilon,\beta,\mu are dimensionless parameters.

As aforementioned, by setting μ=0\mu=0 in (1.1), one recovers the Saint-Venant system, which is an archetype of first-order quasilinear systems of conservation laws. Our strategy in the following is to adapt to the Green-Naghdi equations the well-known techniques — and in particular a priori energy estimates — developed for such systems. Such energy estimates are obviously not guaranteed, due to the presence of the additional third-order nonlinear operators. The key ingredient of this work is the extraction of a quasilinear structure of (1.1), form which energy estimates can be deduced, and eventually a standard Picard iteration scheme can be set up.

Such a “quasilinearization” is also the key ingredient in the proof of the local existence of solutions to the water waves system [31, Theorem 4.16]. However, the structure of the water waves system and the one of the Green-Naghdi system look different, due to the fact that they use different unknowns. Indeed, the second equation in (1.1) describes the time-evolution of the layer-averaged horizontal velocity, while the Zakharov/Craig-Sulem formulation of the water waves system involves the trace of the velocity potential at the surface. To our opinion, the main contribution of this work is the demonstration that when expressed in a different set of variables, the Green-Naghdi system possesses a structure which is very similar to the water waves one; and that one can take advantage of this fact to adapt the proof of the local well-posedness of the latter to the one of the former.

To be more precise, our work is based on another formulation of system (1.1), namely

(1.3) {∂tζ+∇⋅(h​𝐮)=0,(∂t+ϵ𝐮⟂curl)𝐯+∇ζ+ϵ2∇(|𝐮|2)=μϵ∇(ℛ[h,𝐮]+ℛb[h,βb,𝐮]),\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta+\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u})=0,\\ \\ \big(\partial_{t}+\epsilon{\bf u}^{\perp}\curl\big)\mathbf{v}+\nabla\zeta+\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla(\lvert{\bf u}\rvert^{2})=\mu\epsilon\nabla\big(\mathcal{R}[h,{\bf u}]+\mathcal{R}_{b}[h,\beta b,{\bf u}]\big),\end{array}\right.

where we denote curl⁡(v1,v2)=def∂1v2−∂2v1\curl(v_{1},v_{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\partial_{1}v_{2}-\partial_{2}v_{1} and (u1,u2)⟂=def(−u2,u1)(u_{1},u_{2})^{\perp}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}(-u_{2},u_{1}), and

(1.4) ℛ⁡[h,𝐮]\displaystyle\mathcal{R}[h,{\bf u}] =def𝐮3​h⋅∇(h3∇⋅𝐮)+12h2(∇⋅𝐮)2,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{{\bf u}}{3h}\cdot\nabla(h^{3}\nabla\cdot{\bf u})+\frac{1}{2}h^{2}(\nabla\cdot{\bf u})^{2},
(1.5) ℛb​[h,β​b,𝐮]\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{b}[h,\beta b,{\bf u}] =def−12(𝐮h⋅∇(h2(β∇b⋅𝐮))+h(β∇b⋅𝐮)∇⋅𝐮+(β∇b⋅𝐮)2),\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}-\ \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{{\bf u}}{h}\cdot\nabla\big(h^{2}(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u})\big)+h(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u})\nabla\cdot{\bf u}+(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u})^{2}\right),

and 𝐯\mathbf{v} is defined (recalling the definition of the operator 𝒯\mathcal{T} in (1.2)) by

(1.6) h​𝐯=h​𝐮+μ​h​𝒯​[h,β​b]​𝐮=def𝔗⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮.h\mathbf{v}\ =\ h{\bf u}+\mu h\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\ \mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}.

In the following, we study system (1.3) as evolution equations for the variables ζ\zeta and 𝐯\mathbf{v}, with 𝐮=𝐮⁡[h,β​b,𝐯]{\bf u}={\bf u}[h,\beta b,\mathbf{v}] being uniquely defined (see Lemma 2.3 thereafter) by (1.6), and deduce the well-posedness of (1.1) from the one of (1.3).

That system (1.3) is equivalent to (1.1) is certainly not straightforward, and we detail the calculations in Section 6. Physically speaking, the variable 𝐯\mathbf{v} approximates (in the shallow-water regime, μ≪1\mu\ll 1) 𝐯ww=∇ψww\mathbf{v}_{\rm ww}=\nabla\psi_{\rm ww} where ψww\psi_{\rm ww} is the trace of the velocity potential at the surface, and thus system (1.3) is more directly comparable to the water waves system. In particular, the Hamiltonian structure of system (1.3), as brought to light in [25, 36], is a direct counterpart of the celebrated one of the water waves system, and we show in Appendix B how system (1.3) can be quickly derived thanks to the Hamiltonian formalism. This allows to obtain preserved quantities of the system in a straightforward way (see [50] and references therein). Most importantly for our purposes, this allows us to follow the strategy of the proof for the local existence of a solution to the water waves system in [31], and to obtain the corresponding local existence result for system (1.3). More precisely, the variables ζ,𝐯\zeta,\mathbf{v} allow to define the analogue of Alinhac’s “good unknowns” [3] for the water waves system (see e.g. [2]) on which energy estimates can be established. We then extend the analysis so as to prove the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem, in the sense of Hadamard.

After the completion of this work, it was pointed to us that the use of system (1.3) was not necessary (and may be viewed as an over-complicated strategy) to derive a priori energy estimates. For the sake of completeness, we sketch in Appendix A the computations which provide such a priori estimates directly on system (1.1) and would yield an alternative proof of our main results. We still believe that the similarity of structure between the Green-Naghdi system and the one of the water waves system that we exhibit and exploit in this work is an interesting feature. It may serve as a pedagogical tool to get a grasp at some properties of the latter without technical difficulties related to the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator. Incidentally, we do not claim the discovery of formulation (1.3); see [34] and references therein, as well as in Appendix B.

The full justification of the Green-Naghdi system is a consequence of the local existence and uniqueness result for the water waves system ([31, Th. 4.16]), its consistency with the Green-Naghdi system ([31, Prop. 5.8]), the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for the Green-Naghdi system (Theorem 1) as well as a stability result ensuring the Lipschitz dependence of the error with respect to perturbations of the system (Proposition 5.2, thereafter). The following result improves [31, Th. 6.15] by the level of regularity required on the initial data.

Remark 1.1 (Functional setting).

The functional spaces arise as natural energy spaces for the quasilinear structure of system (1.3) that we exhibit in this work. The regularity assumption N≥4N\geq 4 is most certainly not optimal. By the method of our proof, we are restricted to N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, and we cannot hope to obtain a lower threshold than in the pure quasilinear setting, namely N>d/2+1N>d/2+1. That N=3N=3 is not allowed when d=2d=2 comes from technical limitations in various places.

Since our proof is based solely on the structural properties of the system and on energy estimates (in particular, no dispersive estimates are used), it may be adapted almost verbatim to the periodic situation. Although we have not checked all the technical details, we also expect that the strategy may be extended to the more general situation of Kato’s uniformly local Sobolev spaces [29].

Remark 1.2.

Applying the operator curl\curl to (1.3)2\eqref{GN-v}_{2}, one observes the identity

with λ≲|𝐮|HN≤|𝐮|XN\lambda\lesssim\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{H^{N}}\leq\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{N}}. Thus a byproduct of Theorem 1 is that initial smallness of the “generalized vorticity” [39, 23], curl⁡𝐯\curl\mathbf{v}, propagates for large positive times —and remains trivial if it vanishes initially, as in Theorem 2. As already mentioned, the variable 𝐯\mathbf{v} physically approximates ∇ψww\nabla\psi_{\rm ww} where ψww\psi_{\rm ww} is the trace of the velocity potential at the surface. It is therefore physically relevant (although not mathematically required) to assume

curl⁡𝐯=curl⁡(𝐮+μ​𝒯​[h,β​b]​𝐮)≡0.\curl\mathbf{v}=\curl\big({\bf u}+\mu\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}\big)\equiv 0.

This two-dimensional irrotationality condition is a direct consequence of the three-dimensional irrotationality assumption on the velocity flow inside the fluid layer. Outside of this irrotational framework, we believe that the Green-Naghdi system is not a valid model, and refer to [14] for a thorough discussion in this situation.

Outline

The body of the paper is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 1. In Section 2, we provide some technical results concerning our functional spaces and the operator 𝔗\mathfrak{T}. We then exhibit the quasilinear system satisfied by the derivatives of any regular solution to (1.3) in Section 3. This quasilinear formulation allows to obtain a priori energy estimates in Section 4. Finally, we make use of these energy estimates for proving the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for system (1.3) in Section 5. The equivalence between formulation (1.3) and (1.1) is stated in Proposition 6.1. Theorems 1 and 2 follow as direct consequence of the results in Section 5 and Proposition 6.1, and we complete the proofs in Section 6. In Appendix A, we roughly sketch of how energy estimates could be obtained directly on formulation (1.1). For motivation purposes, we also provide a quick discussion on the derivation and Hamiltonian formulation of system (1.3) in Appendix B.

We conclude this section with some independent remarks.

Large time well-posedness and asymptotics

A very natural question in the oceanographic context concerns the large time asymptotic behavior of solutions to the Green-Naghdi system. After a straightforward rescaling of (1.1), the problem is naturally formulated in terms of solutions to the system

(1.8) {∂tζ+1ϵ∇⋅(h𝐮)=0,h=def1+ϵζ−βb,(Id+μ𝒯[h,βb])∂t𝐮+1ϵ∇ζ+(𝐮⋅∇)𝐮+μ(𝒬[h,𝐮]+𝒬b[h,βb,𝐮])=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u})=0,\qquad h\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}1+\epsilon\zeta-\beta b,\\ \\ \big({\rm Id}+\mu\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]\big)\partial_{t}{\bf u}+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\nabla\zeta+({\bf u}\cdot\nabla){\bf u}+\mu\big(\mathcal{Q}[h,{\bf u}]+\mathcal{Q}_{b}[h,\beta b,{\bf u}]\big)=0.\end{array}\right.

Is the Cauchy problem for (1.8) locally well-posed, uniformly with respect to the small parameter ϵ\epsilon? Is it globally well-posed for sufficiently small ϵ\epsilon? Can we exhibit “averaged” equations asymptotically describing the behavior of the solution?

This type of singular limit has been widely studied in particular in the context of the low Mach number limit; see e.g. [21, 1] and references therein. As a matter of fact, when β=μ=0\beta=\mu=0, one recognizes the incompressible limit for the isentropic two-dimensional Euler equations, and it is tempting to elaborate on the analogy. One would then expect the solutions to (1.8) to be asymptotically described (as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0) as the superposition of two components:

  • •

    The “incompressible” component, being defined as the solution to

    (1.9) {∇⋅((1−β​b)​𝐮)=0,(Id+μ𝒯[1−βb,βb])∂t𝐮+(𝐮⋅∇)𝐮+μ(𝒬[1−βb,𝐮]+𝒬b[1−βb,βb,𝐮])=−∇p,\hskip-5.0pt\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\nabla\cdot((1-\beta b){\bf u})=0,\\ \\ \big({\rm Id}+\mu\mathcal{T}[1-\beta b,\beta b]\big)\partial_{t}{\bf u}+({\bf u}\cdot\nabla){\bf u}+\mu\big(\mathcal{Q}[1-\beta b,{\bf u}]+\mathcal{Q}_{b}[1-\beta b,\beta b,{\bf u}]\big)=-\nabla p,\end{array}\right.

    where the “pressure” pp in the right-hand side of (1.9)2\eqref{GN-u-LT-incomp}_{2} is the Lagrange multiplier associated to the “incompressibility” constraint (1.9)1\eqref{GN-u-LT-incomp}_{1}.

  • •

    The “acoustic” component, being defined as the solution to

    (1.10) {∂tζ+1ϵ∇⋅((1−βb)𝐮)=0,(Id+μ𝒯[1−βb,βb])∂t𝐮+1ϵ∇ζ=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\nabla\cdot((1-\beta b){\bf u})=0,\\ \\ \big({\rm Id}+\mu\mathcal{T}[1-\beta b,\beta b]\big)\partial_{t}{\bf u}+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\nabla\zeta=0,\end{array}\right.

    with initial data satisfying curl(𝐮+μ𝒯[1−βb,βb]𝐮)|=t=00\curl({\bf u}+\mu\mathcal{T}[1-\beta b,\beta b]{\bf u})\left|{}_{{}_{t=0}}\right.=0.

The system (1.9) was derived in [12, 13], and is usually referred to as the great-lake equations. Its well-posedness, extending the theory concerning the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations, was subsequently provided in [35, 44]. However, these authors apparently overlooked the role of the irrotationality assumption discussed in Remark 1.2, as the only functions satisfying the constraint (1.9)1\eqref{GN-u-LT-incomp}_{1} as well as the irrotationality condition curl⁡(𝐮+μ​𝒯​[1−β​b,β​b]​𝐮)=0\curl({\bf u}+\mu\mathcal{T}[1-\beta b,\beta b]{\bf u})=0 are in fact trivial. In other words, in the irrotational framework that is the only one for which the Green-Naghdi system is rigorously justified, the incompressible (or rigid-lid) component vanishes; see also [43] for a similar discussion on the water waves system. One thus expects that the flow is asymptotically described by (1.10) only, in the limit ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0.

However, when trying to adapt the usual strategy for rigorously proving such behavior, one immediately encounters a serious difficulty in the physically relevant situation of non-trivial topography, which transpires in the the fact that our lower bound for the existence time in Theorem 1 depends on the size of the bottom variations in addition to the size of the initial data. When transcribed to system (1.8), this means that we are not able to obtain a lower bound on the existence time of its solutions which is uniform with respect to ϵ\epsilon, unless β=𝒪⁡(ϵ)\beta=\mathcal{O}(\epsilon).

For the Saint-Venant system, that is setting μ=0\mu=0, Bresch and Métivier [11] have obtained such a uniform lower bound without any restriction on the amplitude bathymetry. The strategy consists in estimating first the time derivatives of the solution, and then using the system to deduce estimates on space derivatives. A related strategy (in the sense that we look for operators commuting with the singular component of the system) amounts to remark that for any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, one can control the L2L^{2}-norm of

ζn=def(∇⋅(1−b)∇)nζ,𝐮n=def(∇(1−b)∇⋅)n𝐮\zeta_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}(\nabla\cdot(1-b)\nabla)^{n}\zeta,\qquad{\bf u}_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}(\nabla(1-b)\nabla\cdot)^{n}{\bf u}

by exhibiting the quasilinear system satisfied by (ζn,𝐮n)(\zeta_{n},{\bf u}_{n}) and applying simple energy estimates. This allows to control the H2​nH^{2n}-norm of ζ,𝐮\zeta,{\bf u}, provided that the initial data and bottom topography are sufficiently regular. One expects a similar strategy to work for the water waves system (see [40]; partial results have been obtained by the method of time derivatives in [41]), that is to control

ζn=def(1μ​Gμ​[0,β​b])n​ζ,ψn=def(1μ​Gμ​[0,β​b])n​ψ\zeta_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}(\frac{1}{\mu}G^{\mu}[0,\beta b])^{n}\zeta,\qquad\psi_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}(\frac{1}{\mu}G^{\mu}[0,\beta b])^{n}\psi

where GμG^{\mu} is the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator, recalled in Appendix B. Since GμG^{\mu} is an operator of order 11, controlling ζn,ψn\zeta_{n},\psi_{n} indeed allows to control higher regularities on ζ,ψ\zeta,\psi. The strategy however fails for the Green-Naghdi system, as the corresponding operator, namely (see Appendix B)

1μGμ[0,βb]∙≈−∇⋅((1−βb)𝔗[1−βb,βb]−1{(1−βb)∇∙})\frac{1}{\mu}G^{\mu}[0,\beta b]\bullet\approx-\nabla\cdot\Big((1-\beta b)\mathfrak{T}[1-\beta b,\beta b]^{-1}\big\{(1-\beta b)\nabla\bullet\big\}\Big)

is of order 00. One could easily propose different systems that do not suffer from such a shortcoming, by adding the effect of surface tension as in [41], or modifying the system without hurting its consistency as in [42]. This is however out of the scope of the present work, and we leave the question of uniform lower bounds for the existence time of solutions to (1.8) as an open problem.

Other models

We expect that our strategy may be of interest to other models for gravity waves. Since our result holds uniformly with respect to μ∈(0,1)\mu\in(0,1), we easily deduce the well-posedness of the Saint-Venant system. This result is of course a direct application of the standard theory on quasilinear hyperbolic systems [8]. In the other direction, it would be interesting to apply our strategy to the higher-order models derived by Matsuno [38], which enrich the Saint-Venant and Green-Naghdi systems with models of arbitrary high order, while preserving the structure of which we take advantage in this work. Similarly, one can derive models with improved frequency dispersion while preserving the structure of the Green-Naghdi model, by modifying the approximate Hamiltonian in Appendix B. Such a strategy was applied by the authors in the one-dimensional and bilayer situation in [20]. Interestingly, since such models can be tuned to fit the dispersion relation of the water waves system, they do not suffer from the shortcoming described above, so that large-time well-posedness is expected to hold even in the presence of a non-trivial bathymetry.

Let us clarify however that our strategy does not require the Hamiltonian structure, but only exploits the ability to construct “good unknowns” through ζ,𝐯\zeta,\mathbf{v} and their derivatives. Thus even models which are derived through careless approximations may preserve the quasilinear structure which is necessary for our energy estimates. Such is the case for the Boussinesq-Peregrine system (see [45, 31, 42]), which consists in a simplification of the Green-Naghdi system obtained by withdrawing contributions of size 𝒪⁡(μ​ϵ)\mathcal{O}(\mu\epsilon) while keeping 𝒪⁡(μ​β)\mathcal{O}(\mu\beta) ones:

(1.11) {∂tζ+∇⋅(h​𝐮)=0,∂t(𝐮+μ𝒯[1−βb,βb]𝐮)+∇ζ+ϵ(𝐮⋅∇)𝐮=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta+\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u})=0,\\ \\ \partial_{t}\big({\bf u}+\mu\mathcal{T}[1-\beta b,\beta b]{\bf u}\big)+\nabla\zeta+\epsilon({\bf u}\cdot\nabla){\bf u}=0.\end{array}\right.

Because the elliptic operator Id+μ​𝒯​[1−β​b,β​b]{\rm Id}+\mu\mathcal{T}[1-\beta b,\beta b] does not depend on time, solving numerically the Boussinesq-Peregrine system is much less costly than solving the Green-Naghdi system; see [34, 33]. It turns out that the proof of Theorem 1 does extend to the Boussinesq-Peregrine system with straightforward modifications (all on the side of simplification). More precisely, we obtain the well-posedness of system (1.11) after applying the change of variable

(1.12) 𝐯=def𝐮+μ​𝒯​[1−β​b,β​b]​𝐮\mathbf{v}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}{\bf u}+\mu\mathcal{T}[1-\beta b,\beta b]{\bf u}

and extracting the quasilinear system satisfied by ∂αζ\partial^{\alpha}\zeta and ∂α𝐯\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v}.

Theorem 3 (Boussinesq-Peregrine).

Theorem 1 holds replacing system (1.1) with system (1.11). The full justification in the sense of Theorem 2 holds as well, controlling the error as

∀t∈[0,min⁡(T,Tww)],|ζww−ζBP|HN−6+|∇ψww−𝐯BP|YN−6≤𝐂⁡(μ2+μ​ϵ)​t,\forall t\in[0,\min(T,T_{\rm ww})],\qquad\big\lvert\zeta_{\rm ww}-\zeta_{\rm BP}\big\rvert_{H^{N-6}}+\big\lvert\nabla\psi_{\rm ww}-\mathbf{v}_{\rm BP}\big\rvert_{Y^{N-6}}\leq{\bf C}\,(\mu^{2}+\mu\epsilon)\,t,

with ζBP,𝐮BP\zeta_{\rm BP},{\bf u}_{\rm BP} the unique strong solution to (1.11) and 𝐯BP\mathbf{v}_{\rm BP} defined by (1.12).

Compared with [42, Th. 2.1], our result provides a larger lower bound on the time of existence, and does not rely on the assumption ϵ=𝒪⁡(μ)\epsilon=\mathcal{O}(\mu).

2 Preliminary results

In this section, we fix parameters n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, α∈ℕd\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{d} and denote a≲ba\lesssim b for a≤C​ba\leq Cb where CC is a constant depending (non-decreasingly) only on nn, dd, and possibly |α||\alpha| and μ\mu. We denote ⟨A⟩n>r=A\big\langle A\big\rangle_{n>r}=A if n>rn>r and ⟨A⟩n>r=0\big\langle A\big\rangle_{n>r}=0 otherwise, and a∨b=max⁡(a,b)a\vee b=\max(a,b). The results are tailored for the dimension d=2d=2 (through the repeated use of the continuous Sobolev embedding H2⊂L∞H^{2}\subset L^{\infty} for instance) but hold as well when d=1d=1. They are not meant to be sharp, but only sufficient for our needs. The call for “tame” estimates stems from the Bona-Smith technique enforcing continuity properties stated in Proposition 5.3; rougher estimates would be sufficient for the existence and uniqueness of solutions, as in Proposition 5.1.

|f𝐮|Xn≲|f𝐮|Hn+μ|f∇⋅𝐮|Hn+μ|∇f⋅𝐮|Hn,\big\lvert f{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{n}}\lesssim\big\lvert f{\bf u}\big\rvert_{H^{n}}+\sqrt{\mu}\big\lvert f\nabla\cdot{\bf u}\big\rvert_{H^{n}}+\sqrt{\mu}\big\lvert\nabla f\cdot{\bf u}\big\rvert_{H^{n}},

with product estimates (2.4) and (2.5), as well as the continuous embedding (2.1) in Lemma 2.1.

Finally, we notice that f​𝐯∈Y0=(X0)′f\mathbf{v}\in Y^{0}=(X^{0})^{\prime} and |f​𝐯|Y0≲(|f|L∞+|∇f|H2)​|𝐯|(X0)′\big\lvert f\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}\lesssim\big(\big\lvert f\big\rvert_{L^{\infty}}+\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{2}}\big)\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{(X^{0})^{\prime}} since for any 𝐮∈X0{\bf u}\in X^{0},

For n∈{0,1}n\in\{0,1\}, we write

|f​𝐯|Yn+1≲|f​𝐯|Yn+∑|α|=1|f​∂α𝐯|Yn+|(∂αf)​𝐯|Yn≲|f​𝐯|Yn+∑|α|=1|f​∂α𝐯|Yn+|(∂αf)​𝐯|Hn,\big\lvert f\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n+1}}\lesssim\big\lvert f\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}+\sum_{|\alpha|=1}\big\lvert f\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}+\big\lvert(\partial^{\alpha}f)\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}\lesssim\big\lvert f\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}+\sum_{|\alpha|=1}\big\lvert f\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}+\big\lvert(\partial^{\alpha}f)\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{H^{n}},

where we used (2.2) in Lemma 2.1 for the last estimate. Estimate (2.8) follows by finite induction, using (2.4) and again (2.2). For n>2n>2, we use Leibniz rule:

|∂α(f​𝐯)|Y0≤|f​∂α𝐯|Y0+∑β+γ=α|β|≥1,|γ|≥0(αβ)​|(∂βf)​(∂γ𝐯)|Y0.\big\lvert\partial^{\alpha}(f\mathbf{v})\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}\leq\big\lvert f\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta+\gamma=\alpha\\ |\beta|\geq 1,|\gamma|\geq 0\end{subarray}}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v})\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}.

Estimate (2.8) follows from the above bilinear estimate

|(∂βf)​(∂γ𝐯)|Y0≲|(∂βf)​(∂γ𝐯)|L2≤|∇f|H2​|𝐯|Hn−1+|∇f|Hn−1​|𝐯|H2\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v})\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}\lesssim\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v})\big\rvert_{L^{2}}\leq\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{2}}\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{H^{n-1}}+\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{n-1}}\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{H^{2}}

and using again the embedding (2.2). The proof is complete. ∎

Let us now exhibit elliptic estimates concerning the operator 𝔗\mathfrak{T}, defined in (1.2),(1.6).

Lemma 2.3.

Let b∈H˙3​(ℝd)b\in\dot{H}^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and h∈H˙2​(ℝd)h\in\dot{H}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be such that (1.7) holds. Then 𝔗⁡[h,β​b]∈ℒ⁡(X0,(X0)′)\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]\in\mathcal{L}(X^{0};(X^{0})^{\prime}) and is symmetric:

∀𝐮1,𝐮2∈X0,⟨𝔗⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮1,𝐮2⟩(X0)′=⟨𝔗⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮2,𝐮1⟩(X0)′.\forall{\bf u}_{1},{\bf u}_{2}\in X^{0},\quad\big\langle\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}_{1},{\bf u}_{2}\big\rangle_{(X^{0})^{\prime}}\ =\ \big\langle\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}_{2},{\bf u}_{1}\big\rangle_{(X^{0})^{\prime}}.

Moreover, one has

∀𝐮1,𝐮2∈X0,|⟨𝔗⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮1,𝐮2⟩(X0)′|≤C⁡(μ,h⋆,β​|∇b|L∞)​|𝐮1|X0​|𝐮2|X0,\forall{\bf u}_{1},{\bf u}_{2}\in X^{0},\quad\lvert\big\langle\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}_{1},{\bf u}_{2}\big\rangle_{(X^{0})^{\prime}}\rvert\leq C(\mu,h^{\star},\beta\big\lvert\nabla b\big\rvert_{L^{\infty}})\big\lvert{\bf u}_{1}\big\rvert_{X^{0}}\big\lvert{\bf u}_{2}\big\rvert_{X^{0}},
∀𝐮∈X0,|𝐮|X02≤C⁡(h⋆−1)​⟨𝔗⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮,𝐮⟩(X0)′.\forall{\bf u}\in X^{0},\quad\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{0}}^{2}\leq C(h_{\star}^{-1})\big\langle\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u},{\bf u}\big\rangle_{(X^{0})^{\prime}}.

In particular, 𝔗⁡[h,β​b]:X0→(X0)′\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]:X^{0}\to(X^{0})^{\prime} is a topological isomorphism and

∀𝐯∈(X0)′,|𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​𝐯|X0≤C⁡(h⋆−1)​|𝐯|(X0)′.\forall\mathbf{v}\in(X^{0})^{\prime},\quad\big\lvert\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{X^{0}}\leq C(h_{\star}^{-1})\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{(X^{0})^{\prime}}.
Proof.

We establish the estimates for 𝐮,𝐮1,𝐮2∈𝒮​(ℝd)d{\bf u},{\bf u}_{1},{\bf u}_{2}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{d} so that all the terms are well-defined, and the ((X0)′−X0)((X^{0})^{\prime}-X^{0}) duality product coincides with the L2L^{2} inner product. The result for less regular functions is obtained by density of 𝒮​(ℝd)d\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{d} in X0X^{0} and continuous linear extension.

By definition of 𝔗\mathfrak{T} in (1.6) and after integration by parts, one has

(𝔗⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮1,𝐮2)L2=∫ℝdh​𝐮1⋅𝐮2+μ3​h3​(∇⋅𝐮1)​(∇⋅𝐮2)−μ2h2((∇⋅𝐮2)(β∇b⋅𝐮1)+(β∇b⋅𝐮2)(∇⋅𝐮1))+μh(β∇b⋅𝐮1)(β∇b⋅𝐮2),\big(\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}_{1},{\bf u}_{2}\big)_{L^{2}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}h{\bf u}_{1}\cdot{\bf u}_{2}+\frac{\mu}{3}h^{3}(\nabla\cdot{\bf u}_{1})(\nabla\cdot{\bf u}_{2})\\ -\frac{\mu}{2}h^{2}\big((\nabla\cdot{\bf u}_{2})(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u}_{1})+(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u}_{2})(\nabla\cdot{\bf u}_{1})\big)+\mu h(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u}_{1})(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u}_{2}),

from which the symmetry is evident. The first estimate of the Lemma follows by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The second one is obvious when rewriting

(𝔗[h,βb]𝐮,𝐮)L2=∫ℝdh|𝐮|2+μ12h3|∇⋅𝐮|2+μ4h|h∇⋅𝐮−2β∇b⋅𝐮|2.\big(\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u},{\bf u}\big)_{L^{2}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}h\lvert{\bf u}\rvert^{2}+\frac{\mu}{12}h^{3}\lvert\nabla\cdot{\bf u}\rvert^{2}+\frac{\mu}{4}h\lvert h\nabla\cdot{\bf u}-2\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u}\rvert^{2}.

This shows that 𝔗⁡[h,β​b]:X0→(X0)′\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]:X^{0}\to(X^{0})^{\prime} is continuous and coercive, so that the operator version of Lax-Milgram theorem ensures that 𝔗⁡[h,β​b]\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b] is an isomorphism. The continuity of the inverse follows from the coercivity of 𝔗⁡[h,β​b]\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]:

|𝐮|X02≤C⁡(h⋆−1)​|⟨𝔗⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮,𝐮⟩(X0)′|≤C⁡(h⋆−1)​|𝔗⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮|(X0)′​|𝐮|X0,\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{0}}^{2}\leq C(h_{\star}^{-1})\lvert\big\langle\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u},{\bf u}\big\rangle_{(X^{0})^{\prime}}\rvert\leq C(h_{\star}^{-1})\big\lvert\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}\big\rvert_{(X^{0})^{\prime}}\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{0}},

and setting 𝐮=𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​𝐯{\bf u}=\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}\mathbf{v} above. ∎

Lemma 2.4.

Let b∈H˙4​(ℝd)b\in\dot{H}^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and h∈H˙3​(ℝd)h\in\dot{H}^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be such that (1.7) holds; and let 𝐯∈Yn\mathbf{v}\in Y^{n}. Then 𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​𝐯∈Xn\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}\mathbf{v}\in X^{n} and

|𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​𝐯|Xn≤C⁡(μ,h⋆−1,h⋆,|∇h|H2,β​|∇b|H3)​(|𝐯|Yn+⟨|∇h|Hn−1​|𝐯|Y2⟩n>2).\big\lvert\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{X^{n}}\leq C(\mu,h_{\star}^{-1},h^{\star},\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{2}},\beta\big\lvert\nabla b\big\rvert_{H^{3}})\Big(\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}+\big\langle\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{n-1}}\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{2}}\big\rangle_{n>2}\Big).
Proof.

Let 𝐯∈𝒮​(ℝd)d\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{d}, and denote for simplicity 𝔗=def𝔗⁡[h,β​b]\mathfrak{T}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]. One has, for Λn=(Id−Δ)n/2\Lambda^{n}=({\rm Id}-\Delta)^{n/2},

[Λn,𝔗−1]​𝐯=−𝔗−1​Λn​𝔗​𝔗−1​𝐯+𝔗−1​𝔗​Λn​𝔗−1​𝐯=−𝔗−1​[Λn,𝔗]​𝔗−1​𝐯.\big[\Lambda^{n},\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\big]\mathbf{v}=-\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\Lambda^{n}\mathfrak{T}\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}+\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathfrak{T}\Lambda^{n}\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}=-\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\big[\Lambda^{n},\mathfrak{T}\big]\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}.

By definition of 𝔗\mathfrak{T} and since Λn\Lambda^{n} commutes with space differentiation, we have for any 𝐮,𝐰∈𝒮​(ℝd)d{\bf u},\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{d},

|([Λn,𝔗]𝐮,𝐰)L2|=([Λn,h]𝐮,𝐰)L2+μ3([Λn,h3]∇⋅𝐮,∇⋅𝐰)L2−μ2([Λn,h2(β∇b)⋅]𝐮,∇⋅𝐰)L2−μ2([Λn,h2(β∇b)]∇⋅𝐮,𝐰)L2+μ([Λn,h(β∇b)(β∇b)⋅]𝐮,𝐰)L2.\lvert\big(\big[\Lambda^{n},\mathfrak{T}\big]{\bf u},\mathbf{w}\big)_{L^{2}}\rvert=\big(\big[\Lambda^{n},h\big]{\bf u},\mathbf{w}\big)_{L^{2}}+\frac{\mu}{3}\big(\big[\Lambda^{n},h^{3}\big]\nabla\cdot{\bf u},\nabla\cdot\mathbf{w}\big)_{L^{2}}\\ -\frac{\mu}{2}\big([\Lambda^{n},h^{2}(\beta\nabla b)\cdot]{\bf u},\nabla\cdot\mathbf{w}\big)_{L^{2}}-\frac{\mu}{2}\big([\Lambda^{n},h^{2}(\beta\nabla b)]\nabla\cdot{\bf u},\mathbf{w}\big)_{L^{2}}+\mu\big([\Lambda^{n},h(\beta\nabla b)(\beta\nabla b)\cdot]{\bf u},\mathbf{w}\big)_{L^{2}}.

Commutator estimates (see e.g. [31, Corollary B.9]) and product estimate (2.5) yield

|([Λn,𝔗]​𝐮,𝐰)L2|≤C⁡(μ,h⋆,|∇h|H2,β​|∇b|H3)​(|Λn−1​𝐮|X0+⟨|∇h|Hn−1​|Λ2​𝐮|X0⟩n>2)​|𝐰|X0.\lvert\big(\big[\Lambda^{n},\mathfrak{T}\big]{\bf u},\mathbf{w}\big)_{L^{2}}\rvert\leq C(\mu,h^{\star},\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{2}},\beta\big\lvert\nabla b\big\rvert_{H^{3}})\Big(\big\lvert\Lambda^{n-1}{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{0}}+\big\langle\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{n-1}}\big\lvert\Lambda^{2}{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{0}}\big\rangle_{n>2}\Big)\big\lvert\mathbf{w}\big\rvert_{X^{0}}.

By density and continuity arguments, we infer that for any 𝐮∈Xn−1{\bf u}\in X^{n-1}, [Λn,𝔗]​𝐮∈(X0)′\big[\Lambda^{n},\mathfrak{T}\big]{\bf u}\in(X^{0})^{\prime} and

|[Λn,𝔗]​𝐮|(X0)′≤C⁡(μ,h⋆,|∇h|H2,β​|∇b|H3)​(|𝐮|Xn−1+⟨|∇h|Hn−1​|𝐮|X2⟩n>2).\big\lvert\big[\Lambda^{n},\mathfrak{T}\big]{\bf u}\big\rvert_{(X^{0})^{\prime}}\leq C(\mu,h^{\star},\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{2}},\beta\big\lvert\nabla b\big\rvert_{H^{3}})\Big(\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{n-1}}+\big\langle\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{n-1}}\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{2}}\big\rangle_{n>2}\Big).

Combining the above and by Lemma 2.3, we find

|𝔗−1​𝐯|Xn\displaystyle\big\lvert\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{X^{n}} =|𝔗−1​Λn​𝐯−𝔗−1​[Λn,𝔗]​𝔗−1​𝐯|X0≤C⁡(h⋆−1)​|Λn​𝐯−[Λn,𝔗]​𝔗−1​𝐯|(X0)′\displaystyle=\big\lvert\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\Lambda^{n}\mathbf{v}-\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\big[\Lambda^{n},\mathfrak{T}\big]\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{X^{0}}\leq C(h_{\star}^{-1})\big\lvert\Lambda^{n}\mathbf{v}-\big[\Lambda^{n},\mathfrak{T}\big]\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{(X^{0})^{\prime}}
≤C⁡(μ,h⋆−1,h⋆,|∇h|H2,β​|∇b|H3)​(|𝐯|Yn+|𝔗−1​𝐯|Xn−1+⟨|∇h|Hn−1​|𝔗−1​𝐯|X2⟩n>2).\displaystyle\leq C(\mu,h_{\star}^{-1},h^{\star},\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{2}},\beta\big\lvert\nabla b\big\rvert_{H^{3}})\Big(\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}+\big\lvert\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{X^{n-1}}+\big\langle\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{n-1}}\big\lvert\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{X^{2}}\big\rangle_{n>2}\Big).

The result now follows by induction on n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, and by density of 𝒮​(ℝd)d\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{d} in YnY^{n}. ∎

We now exhibit first-order expansions of our operators which are used to obtain the quasilinear formulation of our system, in Proposition 3.1 below.

Lemma 2.5.

For any f,g∈H˙3∨n+|α|−1​(ℝd)f,g\in\dot{H}^{3\vee n+|\alpha|-1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and |α|≥1|\alpha|\geq 1, one has

|∂α(f​g)−f​∂αg|Hn≲|∇f|H2∨n+|α|−1​|g|Hn+|α|−1.\big\lvert\partial^{\alpha}(fg)-f\partial^{\alpha}g\big\rvert_{H^{n}}\lesssim\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{2\vee n+|\alpha|-1}}\big\lvert g\big\rvert_{H^{n+|\alpha|-1}}.
Proof.

Using Leibniz rule, we only have to estimate

|(∂βf)​(∂γg)|L2 for |β|+|γ|≤n+|α| and |β|≥1.\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}g)\big\rvert_{L^{2}}\quad\text{ for $|\beta|+|\gamma|\leq n+|\alpha|$ and $|\beta|\geq 1$}.

If |β|=1|\beta|=1, then |γ|≤n+|α|−1|\gamma|\leq n+|\alpha|-1, and we find by continuous Sobolev embedding H2⊂L∞H^{2}\subset L^{\infty}

|(∂βf)​(∂γg)|L2≤|∂βf|H2​|∂γg|L2.\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}g)\big\rvert_{L^{2}}\leq\big\lvert\partial^{\beta}f\big\rvert_{H^{2}}\big\lvert\partial^{\gamma}g\big\rvert_{L^{2}}.

If |β|=2|\beta|=2, then |γ|≤n+|α|−2|\gamma|\leq n+|\alpha|-2, and standard product estimate (see e.g. [31, Prop. B.2]) yields

|(∂βf)​(∂γg)|L2≤|∂βf|H1​|∂γg|H1.\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}g)\big\rvert_{L^{2}}\leq\big\lvert\partial^{\beta}f\big\rvert_{H^{1}}\big\lvert\partial^{\gamma}g\big\rvert_{H^{1}}.

If |β|>2|\beta|>2, then |γ|≤n+|α|−3|\gamma|\leq n+|\alpha|-3, and we find by continuous Sobolev embedding H2⊂L∞H^{2}\subset L^{\infty}

|(∂βf)​(∂γg)|L2≤|∂βf|L2​|∂γg|H2.\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}g)\big\rvert_{L^{2}}\leq\big\lvert\partial^{\beta}f\big\rvert_{L^{2}}\big\lvert\partial^{\gamma}g\big\rvert_{H^{2}}.

This concludes the proof. ∎

Lemma 2.6.

For any f∈H˙4∨n+|α|−1​(ℝd)f\in\dot{H}^{4\vee n+|\alpha|-1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and 𝐯∈Yn+|α|−1\mathbf{v}\in Y^{n+|\alpha|-1} with n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and |α|≥1|\alpha|\geq 1, one has

|∂α(f​𝐯)−f​∂α𝐯|Yn≲|∇f|H3∨n+|α|−1​|𝐯|Yn+|α|−1.\big\lvert\partial^{\alpha}(f\mathbf{v})-f\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}\lesssim\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{3\vee n+|\alpha|-1}}\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n+|\alpha|-1}}.
Proof.

Using Leibniz rule, we only have to estimate

|(∂βf)​(∂γ𝐯)|Y0 for |β|+|γ|≤n+|α| and |β|≥1.\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v})\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}\quad\text{ for $|\beta|+|\gamma|\leq n+|\alpha|$ and $|\beta|\geq 1$}.

If |β|=1|\beta|=1, then |γ|≤n+|α|−1|\gamma|\leq n+|\alpha|-1, and we use the product estimate (2.8) in Lemma 2.2 to deduce

|(∂βf)​(∂γ𝐯)|Y0≤|∂βf|H3​|∂γ𝐯|Y0.\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v})\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}\leq\big\lvert\partial^{\beta}f\big\rvert_{H^{3}}\big\lvert\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}.

For |β|=2|\beta|=2, |β|=3|\beta|=3 and |β|>3|\beta|>3, we proceed as in the proof of Lemma 2.5, and using (2.2) in Lemma 2.1: by the continuous embedding L2⊂Y0L^{2}\subset Y^{0} we fall into the L2L^{2} setting, and the continuous embedding Yn+|α|−1⊂Hn+|α|−2Y^{n+|\alpha|-1}\subset H^{n+|\alpha|-2} allows to control |∂γ𝐯|H|β|−2≤|∂γ𝐯|Hn+|α|−2\big\lvert\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{H^{|\beta|-2}}\leq\big\lvert\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{H^{n+|\alpha|-2}}. ∎

Lemma 2.7.

For any f,g∈H˙3∨n+|α|−1​(ℝd)f,g\in\dot{H}^{3\vee n+|\alpha|-1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with n∈{0,1}n\in\{0,1\} and |α|≥1|\alpha|\geq 1, one has

|∂α(f​g)−g​∂αf−f​∂αg|Hn≲|∇f|H2​|∇g|Hn+|α|−2+|∇f|Hn+|α|−2​|∇g|H2.\big\lvert\partial^{\alpha}(fg)-g\partial^{\alpha}f-f\partial^{\alpha}g\big\rvert_{H^{n}}\lesssim\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{2}}\big\lvert\nabla g\big\rvert_{H^{n+|\alpha|-2}}+\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{n+|\alpha|-2}}\big\lvert\nabla g\big\rvert_{H^{2}}.
Proof.

The result for n=0n=0 follows from Leibniz rule:

∂α(f​g)−g​∂αf−f​∂αg=∑β+γ=α|β|≥1,|γ|≥1(αβ)⁡(∂βf)​(∂γg),\partial^{\alpha}(fg)-g\partial^{\alpha}f-f\partial^{\alpha}g=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta+\gamma=\alpha\\ |\beta|\geq 1,|\gamma|\geq 1\end{subarray}}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}g),

and we use the standard bilinear estimate for (see [52, Prop. 3.6]) to estimate

|(∂βf)​(∂γg)|L2≲|∇f|L∞​|∇g|H|β|+|γ|−2+|∇f|H|β|+|γ|−2​|∇g|L∞,\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}g)\big\rvert_{L^{2}}\lesssim\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{L^{\infty}}\big\lvert\nabla g\big\rvert_{H^{|\beta|+|\gamma|-2}}+\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{|\beta|+|\gamma|-2}}\big\lvert\nabla g\big\rvert_{L^{\infty}},

together with the continuous embedding H2⊂L∞H^{2}\subset L^{\infty}. The case n=1n=1 is obtained in the same way after differentiating the above identity. ∎

Lemma 2.8.

For any f∈H˙4∨n+|α|−1​(ℝd),𝐯∈Y4∨n+|α|−1f\in\dot{H}^{4\vee n+|\alpha|-1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\mathbf{v}\in Y^{4\vee n+|\alpha|-1} with n∈{0,1}n\in\{0,1\} and |α|≥1|\alpha|\geq 1, one has

|∂α(f​𝐯)−𝐯​∂αf−f​∂α𝐯|Yn≲|∇f|H3​|𝐯|Yn+|α|−1+|∇f|Hn+|α|−2​|𝐯|Y4.\displaystyle\big\lvert\partial^{\alpha}(f\mathbf{v})-\mathbf{v}\partial^{\alpha}f-f\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}\lesssim\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{3}}\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n+|\alpha|-1}}+\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{n+|\alpha|-2}}\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{4}}.
Proof.

If α=1\alpha=1, then the result is obvious. For |α|≥2|\alpha|\geq 2, we use Leibniz rule:

∂α(f​𝐯)−𝐯​∂αf−f​∂α𝐯=∑β+γ=α|β|≥1,|γ|≥1(αβ)⁡(∂βf)​(∂γ𝐯).\partial^{\alpha}(f\mathbf{v})-\mathbf{v}\partial^{\alpha}f-f\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta+\gamma=\alpha\\ |\beta|\geq 1,|\gamma|\geq 1\end{subarray}}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v}).

When |β|=1|\beta|=1, then by (2.8) in Lemma 2.2,

|(∂βf)​(∂γ𝐯)|Y0≲(|∂βf|L∞+|∂β∇f|H2)​|∂γ𝐯|Y0≲|∇f|H3​|𝐯|Y|α|−1.\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v})\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}\lesssim\big(\big\lvert\partial^{\beta}f\big\rvert_{L^{\infty}}+\big\lvert\partial^{\beta}\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{2}})\big\lvert\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}\lesssim\big\lvert\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{3}}\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{|\alpha|-1}}.

When |β|≥2|\beta|\geq 2, we use the standard bilinear estimate as above:

|(∂βf)(∂γ𝐯)|L2≲|Λ∇f|L∞|Λ𝐯|H|β|+|γ|−3+|Λ∇f|H|β|+|γ|−3|Λ𝐯|L∞.\big\lvert(\partial^{\beta}f)(\partial^{\gamma}\mathbf{v})\big\rvert_{L^{2}}\lesssim\big\lvert\Lambda\nabla f\big\rvert_{L^{\infty}}\big\lvert\Lambda\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{H^{|\beta|+|\gamma|-3}}+\big\lvert\Lambda\nabla f\big\rvert_{H^{|\beta|+|\gamma|-3}}\big\lvert\Lambda\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{L^{\infty}}.

This yields the desired estimate for n=0n=0, by continuous embedding H2⊂L∞H^{2}\subset L^{\infty} and (2.2) in Lemma 2.1. The case n=1n=1 is obtained similarly. ∎

The following Lemmata exhibit the shape derivatives of the operators 𝔗\mathfrak{T} and 𝔗−1\mathfrak{T}^{-1}.

with

(2.9) dh𝔗[h,βb](f,𝐮)=deff𝐮−μ∇(h2f∇⋅𝐮)+μ∇(fh(β∇b)⋅𝐮)−μfh(β∇b)∇⋅𝐮.{\rm d}_{h}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b](f,{\bf u})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}f{\bf u}-\mu\nabla(h^{2}f\nabla\cdot{\bf u})+\mu\nabla\big(fh(\beta\nabla b)\cdot{\bf u}\big)-\mu fh(\beta\nabla b)\nabla\cdot{\bf u}.

⟨Λn​𝐫,𝐰⟩(X0)′\displaystyle\big\langle\Lambda^{n}{\bf r},\mathbf{w}\big\rangle_{(X^{0})^{\prime}} =(Λn​{∂α(h​𝐮)−h​∂α𝐮−ϵ​∂αζ​𝐮},𝐰)L2\displaystyle=\big(\Lambda^{n}\{\partial^{\alpha}(h{\bf u})-h\partial^{\alpha}{\bf u}-\epsilon\partial^{\alpha}\zeta{\bf u}\},\mathbf{w}\big)_{L^{2}}

|∂α(ζ​𝐮)−ζ​∂α𝐮−∂αζ​𝐮|Hn≲|∇ζ|H2​|𝐮|Hn+|α|−1+|∇ζ|Hn+|α|−2​|𝐮|H3\big\lvert\partial^{\alpha}(\zeta{\bf u})-\zeta\partial^{\alpha}{\bf u}-\partial^{\alpha}\zeta{\bf u}\big\rvert_{H^{n}}\lesssim\big\lvert\nabla\zeta\big\rvert_{H^{2}}\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{H^{n+|\alpha|-1}}+\big\lvert\nabla\zeta\big\rvert_{H^{n+|\alpha|-2}}\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{H^{3}}

and by Lemma 2.5,

and (2.1) in Lemma 2.1 allows to complete the estimate of the first contribution. The other terms are treated similarly, using first Lemma 2.5 to commute the differentiation operator with bottom contributions, product estimates (2.4) and (2.5) to estimate the commutator, and then Lemma 2.7 to deal with surface contributions.

Altogether, one finds that |𝐫1|Hn\big\lvert{\bf r}^{1}\big\rvert_{H^{n}} and |𝐫2|Hn\big\lvert{\bf r}^{2}\big\rvert_{H^{n}} are estimated as in the statement. By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and duality, we deduce that 𝐫∈Yn{\bf r}\in Y^{n} and |𝐫|Yn\big\lvert{\bf r}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}} satisfies the same estimate. The result for 𝐮∈X3∨n+|α|−1{\bf u}\in X^{3\vee n+|\alpha|-1} follows by density and continuous linear extension. ∎

Lemma 2.10.

with dh​𝔗​[h,β​b]{\rm d}_{h}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b] defined in (2.9).

with the notation 𝐮=def𝔗−1​𝐯{\bf u}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathfrak{T}^{-1}\mathbf{v}. By Lemma 2.4 and Lemma 2.9, one has

≤C⁡(μ,h⋆−1,h⋆)​F​(β​|∇b|H3∨n+|α|,ϵ​|∇ζ|H2,ϵ​|𝐮|X3)​(|∇ζ|Hn+|α|−2+|𝐮|Xn+|α|−1)\displaystyle\leq C(\mu,h_{\star}^{-1},h^{\star})F(\beta\big\lvert\nabla b\big\rvert_{H^{3\vee n+|\alpha|}},\epsilon\big\lvert\nabla\zeta\big\rvert_{H^{2}},\epsilon\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{3}})\Big(\big\lvert\nabla\zeta\big\rvert_{H^{n+|\alpha|-2}}+\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{n+|\alpha|-1}}\Big)

We conclude this section with the following result which is essential for estimating the difference between two approximate solutions (in later Proposition 5.2 for instance).

Lemma 2.11.

≤ϵ​C​(|∇h|H2∨n−1,|∇h~|H2∨n−1)​|𝐮|X2∨n​|ζ−ζ~|Hn.\displaystyle\leq\epsilon\,C(\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{2\vee n-1}},\big\lvert\nabla\widetilde{h}\big\rvert_{H^{2\vee n-1}})\big\lvert{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{2\vee n}}\big\lvert\zeta-\widetilde{\zeta}\big\rvert_{H^{n}}.

3 The quasilinear system

The result below is the key ingredient of our proof. We extract the quasilinear structure of system (1.3) in terms of “good unknowns”, from which energy estimates will be deduced in subsequent Section 4. The strategy consists in differentiating system (1.3) several times, and estimate lower order contributions thanks to the formulas obtained in Section 2. However, in order not too break the structure of the first equation, we are led (as for the water waves system [31]) to introduce an appropriate velocity variable which is a combination of the original variables and their derivatives.

Proposition 3.1.

Let α\alpha be a non-zero multi-index and ζ∈H4∨|α|​(ℝd),b∈H˙5∨|α|+2​(ℝd)\zeta\in H^{4\vee|\alpha|}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),b\in\dot{H}^{5\vee|\alpha|+2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be such that (1.7) holds, and 𝐯∈Y4∨|α|\mathbf{v}\in Y^{4\vee|\alpha|}, satisfying (1.3). Denote

(3.1) ζ(α)=def∂αζ and 𝐯(α)=def∂α𝐯−μϵ∇(w∂αζ) where w=def−h∇⋅𝐮+β∇b⋅𝐮.\zeta_{(\alpha)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\partial^{\alpha}\zeta\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v}-\mu\epsilon\,\nabla(w\partial^{\alpha}\zeta)\quad\text{ where }\quad w\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}-h\nabla\cdot{\bf u}+\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u}.

Then ζ(α),𝐯(α)\zeta_{(\alpha)},\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)} satisfy

(3.2) {∂tζ(α)+ϵ∇⋅(𝐮ζ(α))+∇⋅(h𝐮(α))=r(α)(∂t+ϵ𝐮⟂curl)𝐯(α)+∇ζ(α)+ϵ∇(𝐮⋅𝐯(α))=𝐫(α)\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta_{(\alpha)}+\epsilon\nabla\cdot({\bf u}\zeta_{(\alpha)})+\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u}_{(\alpha)})=r_{(\alpha)}\\ \\ (\partial_{t}+\epsilon{\bf u}^{\perp}\curl)\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)}+\nabla\zeta_{(\alpha)}+\epsilon\nabla({\bf u}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)})={\bf r}_{(\alpha)}\end{array}\right.

where we denote

𝐮=def𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​(h​𝐯) and 𝐮(α)=def𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​(h​𝐯(α)),{\bf u}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}(h\mathbf{v})\quad\text{ and }\quad{\bf u}_{(\alpha)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}(h\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)}),

and r(α),𝐫(α)r_{(\alpha)},{\bf r}_{(\alpha)} satisfy the estimates

(3.3) |r(α)|L2+|𝐫(α)|Y0≤𝐅⁡(|ζ|H|α|+|𝐯|Y|α|+|curl⁡𝐯|H|α|−1)\big\lvert r_{(\alpha)}\big\rvert_{L^{2}}+\big\lvert{\bf r}_{(\alpha)}\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}\leq{\bf F}\ \left(\big\lvert\zeta\big\rvert_{H^{|\alpha|}}+\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{|\alpha|}}+\big\lvert\curl\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{H^{|\alpha|-1}}\right)

with 𝐅=C⁡(μ,h⋆−1,h⋆)​F​(β​|∇b|H4∨|α|+1,ϵ​|∇ζ|H3,ϵ​|𝐯|Y4,ϵ​|curl⁡𝐯|H3){\bf F}=C(\mu,h_{\star}^{-1},h^{\star})F\big(\beta\big\lvert\nabla b\big\rvert_{H^{4\vee|\alpha|+1}},\epsilon\big\lvert\nabla\zeta\big\rvert_{H^{3}},\epsilon\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{4}},\epsilon\big\lvert\curl\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{H^{3}}\big).

Moreover, if we denote ζ~,𝐯~\widetilde{\zeta},\widetilde{\mathbf{v}} satisfying the same assumptions and r~(α),𝐫~(α)\widetilde{r}_{(\alpha)},\widetilde{\bf r}_{(\alpha)} the corresponding residuals, then one has

(3.4) |r(α)−r~(α)|L2+|𝐫(α)−𝐫~(α)|Y0≤𝐅~​(|ζ−ζ~|H|α|+|𝐯−𝐯~|Y|α|+|curl⁡𝐯−curl⁡𝐯~|H|α|−1)\big\lvert r_{(\alpha)}-\widetilde{r}_{(\alpha)}\big\rvert_{L^{2}}+\big\lvert{\bf r}_{(\alpha)}-\widetilde{\bf r}_{(\alpha)}\big\rvert_{Y^{0}}\leq\widetilde{\bf F}\ \left(\big\lvert\zeta-\widetilde{\zeta}\big\rvert_{H^{|\alpha|}}+\big\lvert\mathbf{v}-\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{Y^{|\alpha|}}+\big\lvert\curl\mathbf{v}-\curl\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{H^{|\alpha|-1}}\right)

with

𝐅~=C(μ,h⋆−1,h⋆)F(β|∇b|H4∨|α|+1,ϵ|ζ|H4∨|α|,ϵ|𝐯|Y4∨|α|,ϵ|curl𝐯|H3∨|α|−1,OPENϵ​|ζ~|H4∨|α|,ϵ​|𝐯~|Y4∨|α|,ϵ​|curl⁡𝐯~|H3∨|α|−1).\widetilde{\bf F}=C(\mu,h_{\star}^{-1},h^{\star})F\big(\beta\big\lvert\nabla b\big\rvert_{H^{4\vee|\alpha|+1}},\epsilon\big\lvert\zeta\big\rvert_{H^{4\vee|\alpha|}},\epsilon\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{4\vee|\alpha|}},\epsilon\big\lvert\curl\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{H^{3\vee|\alpha|-1}},\\ \epsilon\big\lvert\widetilde{\zeta}\big\rvert_{H^{4\vee|\alpha|}},\epsilon\big\lvert\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{Y^{4\vee|\alpha|}},\epsilon\big\lvert\curl\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{H^{3\vee|\alpha|-1}}\big).
Remark 3.2.

One recovers the quasilinear structure of the water waves system, as exhibited in [31, Sec. 4.2], up to two differences. Firstly, the advection velocity is 𝐮{\bf u} instead of UU (using the notation introduced in Appendix B). This was to be expected, comparing the formulation of the Green-Naghdi system (B.11) with the corresponding formulation of the water waves system (B.12).

Secondly, from the comparison of the aforementioned formulations, one would expect (3.2)2\eqref{GN-quasi}_{2} to exhibit a component of the form

∇(𝔞​ζ) with 𝔞=def1+μ​ϵ​∂tw+μ​ϵ2​V⋅∇w,\nabla(\mathfrak{a}\zeta)\quad\text{ with }\quad\mathfrak{a}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}1+\mu\epsilon\partial_{t}w+\mu\epsilon^{2}V\cdot\nabla w,

with the hyperbolicity condition 𝔞>0\mathfrak{a}>0 accounting for the Rayleigh-Taylor criterion, (−∂zP)z=ϵ​ζ>0{(-\partial_{z}P)_{z=\epsilon\zeta}>0}; see the discussion in [31, Sec. 4.3.5]. In our system, we simply set 𝔞≡1\mathfrak{a}\equiv 1 since the additional contributions can be discarded, thanks to our energy norm and the μ\mu prefactor, by (2.3) in Lemma 2.1. In other words, using the notation of the proof below, one can check that

∇ζ(α)∼Y0∇((1+μϵ(∂t+ϵ𝐮⋅∇)w)ζ(α)).\nabla\zeta_{(\alpha)}\sim_{Y^{0}}\nabla\Big(\big(1+\mu\epsilon(\partial_{t}+\epsilon{\bf u}\cdot\nabla)w\big)\zeta_{(\alpha)}\Big).

Thus the Rayleigh-Taylor criterion for water waves, which is automatically satisfied for small values of the parameter μ\mu, disappears in the Green-Naghdi system (for any values of μ\mu).

∂t𝐯(α)\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)} ∼Y0−∂α∇ζ−ϵ∇(𝐮⋅∂α𝐯)−ϵ𝐮⟂(curl∂α𝐯)+μϵ2∇(𝐮⋅∇(wζ(α)))\displaystyle\sim_{Y^{0}}-\partial^{\alpha}\nabla\zeta-\epsilon\nabla({\bf u}\cdot\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v})-\epsilon{\bf u}^{\perp}(\curl\partial^{\alpha}\mathbf{v})+\mu\epsilon^{2}\nabla({\bf u}\cdot\nabla(w\zeta_{(\alpha)}))
(3.8) =−∂α∇ζ−ϵ∇(𝐮⋅𝐯(α))−ϵ𝐮⟂(curl𝐯(α)).\displaystyle=-\partial^{\alpha}\nabla\zeta-\epsilon\nabla({\bf u}\cdot\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)})-\epsilon{\bf u}^{\perp}(\curl\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)}).

The second estimate of the statement is obtained identically. Since all contributions on the remainders involve either products or the operator 𝔗−1\mathfrak{T}^{-1}, we can express the difference as a sum of terms of the same form but involving at least once ζ−ζ~\zeta-\widetilde{\zeta} or 𝐯−𝐯~\mathbf{v}-\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}, or estimated by Lemma 2.11. |h​𝐯−h~​𝐯~|Yn≤|h⁡(𝐯−𝐯~)|Yn+ϵ​|(ζ−ζ~)​𝐯~|Yn≤C⁡(μ,h⋆,|∇h|H2∨n−1,ϵ​|𝐯~|Y3∨n)​(|𝐯−𝐯~|Yn+|ζ−ζ~|Hn).\big\lvert h\mathbf{v}-\widetilde{h}\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}\leq\big\lvert h(\mathbf{v}-\widetilde{\mathbf{v}})\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}+\epsilon\big\lvert(\zeta-\widetilde{\zeta})\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}\leq C(\mu,h^{\star},\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{2\vee{n-1}}},\epsilon\big\lvert\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{Y^{3\vee n}})\big(\big\lvert\mathbf{v}-\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}+\big\lvert\zeta-\widetilde{\zeta}\big\rvert_{H^{n}}\big).

|𝐮−𝐮~|Xn≤C⁡(μ,h⋆−1,h⋆,|∇b|H3∨n,|∇h|H2∨n−1,|∇h~|H2∨n−1,ϵ​|𝐯|Y2∨n,ϵ​|𝐯~|Y3∨n)×(|𝐯−𝐯~|Yn+|ζ−ζ~|Hn).\big\lvert{\bf u}-\widetilde{\bf u}\big\rvert_{X^{n}}\leq C(\mu,h_{\star}^{-1},h^{\star},\big\lvert\nabla b\big\rvert_{H^{3\vee n}},\big\lvert\nabla h\big\rvert_{H^{2\vee{n-1}}},\big\lvert\nabla\widetilde{h}\big\rvert_{H^{2\vee{n-1}}},\epsilon\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{2\vee n}},\epsilon\big\lvert\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{Y^{3\vee n}})\\ \times\big(\big\lvert\mathbf{v}-\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}+\big\lvert\zeta-\widetilde{\zeta}\big\rvert_{H^{n}}\big).

It is now a tedious but straightforward task to follow the steps of the proof and check that the estimate (3.4) holds. ∎

4 A priori energy estimates

This section is dedicated to a priori energy estimates on the quasilinearized system (3.2) (or rather a mollified version; see below), which we make use in the proof of the existence and uniqueness of solutions to system (1.3) in subsequent Section 5. It is convenient to introduce the following notation, for n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}:

ℰn​(ζ,𝐯)=def|ζ|Hn2+|𝐯|Yn2.\mathcal{E}^{n}(\zeta,\mathbf{v})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\big\lvert\zeta\big\rvert_{H^{n}}^{2}+\big\lvert\mathbf{v}\big\rvert_{Y^{n}}^{2}.

We wish to show that regularity induced by ℰn\mathcal{E}^{n} is propagated by the flow of the Green-Naghdi system (1.3) provided nn is chosen sufficiently large. However, the natural energy of our system is determined by the symmetrizer associated with the quasilinear system (3.2) satisfied by ζ(α),𝐯(α)\zeta_{(\alpha)},\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)}. This leads us to define

ℱn​(ζ,𝐯)=def∑0≤|α|≤nℱ⁡[h,β​b]​(ζ(α),𝐯(α)).\mathcal{F}^{n}(\zeta,\mathbf{v})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\sum_{0\leq|\alpha|\leq n}\mathcal{F}[h,\beta b](\zeta_{(\alpha)},\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)}).

with ζ(α),𝐯(α)\zeta_{(\alpha)},\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)} given by (3.1) and

ℱ⁡[h,β​b]​(ζ(α),𝐯(α))=def|ζ(α)|L22+⟨𝐯(α),h​𝐮(α)⟩(X0)′,\mathcal{F}[h,\beta b](\zeta_{(\alpha)},\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\big\lvert\zeta_{(\alpha)}\big\rvert_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big\langle\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)},h{\bf u}_{(\alpha)}\big\rangle_{(X^{0})^{\prime}},

where we recall that 𝐮(α)=def𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​(h​𝐯(α)){\bf u}_{(\alpha)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}(h\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)}). By convention, we denote ζ(0)=defζ\zeta_{(0)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\zeta and 𝐯(0)=def𝐯\mathbf{v}_{(0)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathbf{v}. In the following, we simply denote ℱ⁡(ζ(α),𝐯(α))=ℱ⁡[h,β​b]​(ζ(α),𝐯(α))\mathcal{F}(\zeta_{(\alpha)},\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)})=\mathcal{F}[h,\beta b](\zeta_{(\alpha)},\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)}) for the sake of readability.

It is not obvious that controlling ℱ⁡(ζ(α),𝐯(α))\mathcal{F}(\zeta_{(\alpha)},\mathbf{v}_{(\alpha)}) for 0≤|α|≤n0\leq|\alpha|\leq n allows to control ℰn​(ζ,𝐯)\mathcal{E}^{n}(\zeta,\mathbf{v}) and conversely, and this is what we investigate in the following Lemmas.

Lemma 4.1.

Proposition 5.3 (Well-posedness).

Under the hypotheses of Proposition 5.1, the unique strong solution to (1.3) satisfies (ζ,𝐯,curl⁡𝐯)∈C⁡([0,T],HN×YN×HN−1)(\zeta,\mathbf{v},\curl\mathbf{v})\in C([0,T];H^{N}\times Y^{N}\times H^{N-1}). The continuity of the flow map follows from the above limits and triangular inequality. ∎

6 Proof of the main results

We proved in the previous section the well-posedness and stability of the Cauchy problem for system (1.3). We show in this section how to transcribe these results to the original formulation of the Green-Naghdi system (1.1). It is claimed in [12, 38] that (1.3) and (1.1) are equivalent, after “judiciously differentiating by parts” and “lengthy calculations”. Since this fact is of considerable importance in our work and is rather tedious to check, we detail the calculations below. We then conclude this section with the proof of Theorems 1 and 2.

Proposition 6.1.

Let b∈H˙5​(ℝd)b\in\dot{H}^{5}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and ζ∈C0​([0,T],H4​(ℝd))\zeta\in C^{0}([0,T];H^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d})) be such that (1.7) holds.

If 𝐮∈C0​([0,T],X4){\bf u}\in C^{0}([0,T];X^{4}) is such that (ζ,𝐮)(\zeta,{\bf u}) satisfies (1.1), then 𝐯=defh−1​𝔗​[h,β​b]​𝐮∈C0​([0,T],Y4)\mathbf{v}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}h^{-1}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}\in C^{0}([0,T];Y^{4}) is uniquely defined and (ζ,𝐯)(\zeta,\mathbf{v}) satisfies (1.3).

If 𝐯∈C0​([0,T],Y4)\mathbf{v}\in C^{0}([0,T];Y^{4}) is such that (ζ,𝐯)(\zeta,\mathbf{v}) satisfies (1.3), then 𝐮=def𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​(h​𝐯)∈C0​([0,T],X4){\bf u}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}(h\mathbf{v})\in C^{0}([0,T];X^{4}) is uniquely defined and (ζ,𝐮)(\zeta,{\bf u}) satisfies (1.1).

Conversely, that 𝐮=def𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​(h​𝐯){\bf u}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}(h\mathbf{v}) is well-defined and 𝐮∈C0​([0,T],X4){\bf u}\in C^{0}([0,T];X^{4}) follows by Lemmata 2.3 and 2.4. Proof of Theorem 1

Appendix B Derivation of the Green-Naghdi system

Our work is based on a non-standard formulation of the Green-Naghdi system. We would like to motivate the relevance of this formulation (the verification of the equivalence between the different formulations is provided in Proposition 6.1). Below, we formally derive the non-standard formulation of the Green-Naghdi system from the Hamiltonian formulation of the water waves system, by approximating the associated Hamiltonian functional. This study, which was essentially provided in [12], has the advantage of revealing in a very straightforward way the Hamiltonian structure of the non-standard formulation of the Green-Naghdi system (and therefore the associated conservation laws) and giving a natural physical interpretation of the variables at stake.

Let us first recall the canonical Hamiltonian structure of the water waves system as brought to light by [54] and Craig-Sulem [19, 18]. Define the following Hamiltonian functional

(B.1) ℋ⁡(ζ,ψ)=def12​∫ℝdζ2+1μ​ψ​Gμ​[ϵ​ζ,β​b]​ψ\mathcal{H}(\zeta,\psi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\zeta^{2}+\frac{1}{\mu}\psi\,G^{\mu}[\epsilon\zeta,\beta b]\psi

where ψ⁡(t,X)=ϕ⁡(t,X,ϵ​ζ​(t,X))\psi(t,X)=\phi(t,X,\epsilon\zeta(t,X)) is the trace of the velocity potential at the surface, and GμG^{\mu} is the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator, defined by

Gμ:φ↦1+μ|ϵ∇ζ|2(∂nϕ)|=z=ϵ​ζ(∂zϕ)|−z=ϵ​ζμ(ϵ∇ζ)⋅(∇Xϕ)|,z=ϵ​ζG^{\mu}:\varphi\mapsto\sqrt{1+\mu|\epsilon\nabla\zeta|^{2}}(\partial_{n}\phi)\left|{}_{{}_{z=\epsilon\zeta}}\right.=(\partial_{z}\phi)\left|{}_{{}_{z=\epsilon\zeta}}\right.-\mu(\epsilon\nabla\zeta)\cdot(\nabla_{X}\phi)\left|{}_{{}_{z=\epsilon\zeta}}\right.,

where ϕ\phi is the unique solution (see e.g. [31] for a detailed and rigorous analysis) to

(B.2) {μΔXϕ+∂z2ϕ=0 in {(X,z)∈ℝd+1,−1+βb(X)≤z≤ϵζ(X)},ϕ(X,ϵζ(X))=φand (∂zϕ−μ(β∇b)⋅(∇Xϕ))(X,−1+βb(X))=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\mu\Delta_{X}\phi+\partial_{z}^{2}\phi=0\quad\text{ in }\{(X,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1},\ -1+\beta b(X)\leq z\leq\epsilon\zeta(X)\},\\ \phi(X,\epsilon\zeta(X))=\varphi\quad\text{and }\quad(\partial_{z}\phi-\mu(\beta\nabla b)\cdot(\nabla_{X}\phi))(X,-1+\beta b(X))=0.\end{array}\right.

The operator GμG^{\mu} is well-defined provided h=def1+ϵ​ζ−β​b≥h⋆>0h\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}1+\epsilon\zeta-\beta b\geq h_{\star}>0, and one can then show that the Zakharov/Craig-Sulem formulation of the water waves system simply reads

(B.3) ∂t(ζψ)=(0Id−Id0)​(δζ​ℋδψ​ℋ).\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}\zeta\\ \psi\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&{\rm Id}\\ -{\rm Id}&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\delta_{\zeta}\mathcal{H}\\ \delta_{\psi}\mathcal{H}\end{pmatrix}.

If one reformulates (in dimension d=2d=2) the above system using, instead of the canonical variables (ζ,ψ)(\zeta,\psi), the variables ζ\zeta and 𝐯=(v1,v2)⊤=def∇ψ\mathbf{v}=(v_{1},v_{2})^{\top}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\nabla\psi, then one obtains

(B.4) ∂t(ζv1v2)=−(0∂1∂2∂10−q∂2q0)​(δζ​ℋδv1​ℋδv2​ℋ).\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}\zeta\\ v_{1}\\ v_{2}\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}0&\partial_{1}&\partial_{2}\\ \partial_{1}&0&-q\\ \partial_{2}&q&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\delta_{\zeta}\mathcal{H}\\ \delta_{v_{1}}\mathcal{H}\\ \delta_{v_{2}}\mathcal{H}\end{pmatrix}.

where q=curl⁡𝐯hq=\frac{\curl\mathbf{v}}{h}. Of course, in our situation, q≡0q\equiv 0 since 𝐯=∇ψ\mathbf{v}=\nabla\psi, but this contribution is kept for the analogy with the Euler or Saint-Venant Hamiltonian formalism ; see e.g. [49]. Keeping this contribution turns out to be necessary for comparing with the standard formulation of the Green-Naghdi system in the general setting; see Proposition 6.1.

Recall that one has the identity [31, Prop. 3.35]

(B.5) 1μGμ[ϵζ,βb]ψ=−∇⋅(h𝐮),𝐮=def11+ϵ​ζ−β​b∫−1+β​bϵ​ζ∇Xϕ(⋅,z)dz.\frac{1}{\mu}G^{\mu}[\epsilon\zeta,\beta b]\psi\ =\ -\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u}),\qquad{\bf u}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{1}{1+\epsilon\zeta-\beta b}\int_{-1+\beta b}^{\epsilon\zeta}\nabla_{X}\phi(\cdot,z)\ {\rm d}z.

so that the first equation in (B.3) or (B.4) simply reads

∂tζ+∇⋅(h​𝐮)=0,\partial_{t}\zeta+\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u})=0,

which is the first equation of the Green-Naghdi system. The system is then completed by constructing an evolution equation for 𝐮{\bf u}, containing only differential operators, which is approximately satisfied by exact solutions of the water waves system, through asymptotic expansions with respect to μ→0\mu\to 0. This equation has different equivalent formulations in the literature as the equations have been rediscovered several times; in this paper we use (1.1), originating from [32, (26)] and justified in the sense of consistency in [31, Prop. 5.8].

Our strategy here is different: we obtain equations written with the original variables ζ,ψ\zeta,\psi (or ζ,𝐯\zeta,\mathbf{v}) by using an asymptotic expansion of the Hamiltonian functional ℋ\mathcal{H}, and plugging it in (B.3) or (B.4). The strategy of deriving the Green-Naghdi system using an approximate Hamiltonian functional or Lagrangian is not new: it was already used in particular in [53, 17] (leading however to an ill-posed system of Green-Naghdi type) and in [39] to derive the original Green-Naghdi system; see also [12, 30, 15, 16].

Let us recall the Dirichlet-to-Neumann expansion [31, Remark 3.39]

(B.6) 1μGμ[ϵζ,βb]ψ=−∇⋅(h∇ψ)+μ∇⋅(h𝒯[h,βb]∇ψ)+𝒪(μ2)\frac{1}{\mu}G^{\mu}[\epsilon\zeta,\beta b]\psi=-\nabla\cdot(h\nabla\psi)+\mu\nabla\cdot(h\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]\nabla\psi\big)+\mathcal{O}(\mu^{2})

with the notation

𝒯[h,b]V=def−13​h∇(h3∇⋅V)+12​h(∇(h2∇b⋅V)−h2∇b∇⋅V)+∇b(∇b⋅V).\mathcal{T}[h,b]V\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{-1}{3h}\nabla(h^{3}\nabla\cdot V)+\frac{1}{2h}\Big(\nabla\big(h^{2}\nabla b\cdot V\big)-h^{2}\nabla b\nabla\cdot V\Big)+\nabla b(\nabla b\cdot V).

It would therefore be natural to consider the approximate Hamiltonian functional from (B.1)

ℋ(ζ,ψ)≈12∫ℝdζ2+ψ(−∇⋅(h∇ψ)+μ∇⋅(h𝒯[h,βb]∇ψ)).\mathcal{H}(\zeta,\psi)\approx\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\zeta^{2}+\psi\Big(-\nabla\cdot(h\nabla\psi)+\mu\nabla\cdot(h\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]\nabla\psi\big)\Big).

However, plugging this approximation into (B.3) or (B.4) yields an ill-posed system (in the sense that the linearized system around the trivial solution ζ=0,ψ=0\zeta=0,\psi=0, in the flat-bottom case, exhibits unstable modes whose amplitude grows exponentially and arbitrarily rapidly for large frequencies). It is interesting to note that the obtained system corresponds to the one exhibited in [53, (10)-(11)] and [17, (14)-(15)] (in the one-dimension and flat-bottom situation) and, as pointed out in [39, (1.8a),(1.8b)], it reduces to the original (ill-posed) Boussinesq system when the amplitude is small, that is withdrawing 𝒪⁡(μ​ϵ)\mathcal{O}(\mu\epsilon) terms.

The ill-posedness of the aforementioned systems can be traced back from the fact that the approximate Hamiltonian functional is no longer positive, whereas the original one is; see [31, Prop. 3.9 and 3.12]. This issue can be avoided as follows: by (B.5) and (B.6), one has

𝐮=∇ψ−μ𝒯[h,βb]∇ψ+𝒪(μ2),thus∇ψ=𝐮+μ𝒯[h,βb]𝐮+𝒪(μ2).{\bf u}=\nabla\psi-\mu\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]\nabla\psi+\mathcal{O}(\mu^{2}),\quad\text{thus}\quad\nabla\psi={\bf u}+\mu\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}+\mathcal{O}(\mu^{2}).

Now, we notice that the operator 𝔗⁡[h,β​b]\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b] defined by

𝔗⁡[h,β​b]​𝐮=defh​𝐮+μ​h​𝒯​[h,β​b]​𝐮\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}\ \stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\ h{\bf u}+\mu h\mathcal{T}[h,\beta b]{\bf u}

is a topological isomorphism (see Lemma 2.3), and therefore

(B.7) 𝐮=𝔗[h,βb]−1(h∇ψ)+𝒪(μ2).{\bf u}=\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}(h\nabla\psi)+\mathcal{O}(\mu^{2}).

It is now natural to use the following approximation:

(B.8) ℋ(ζ,ψ)=12∫ℝdζ2+(∇ψ)⋅(h𝐮)≈12∫ℝdζ2+(h∇ψ)⋅𝔗[h,βb]−1(h∇ψ)=defℋGN(ζ,ψ).\mathcal{H}(\zeta,\psi)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\zeta^{2}+(\nabla\psi)\cdot(h{\bf u})\approx\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\zeta^{2}+(h\nabla\psi)\cdot\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}(h\nabla\psi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathcal{H}_{\rm GN}(\zeta,\psi).

Now, plugging the new approximate Hamiltonian in (B.3) and (B.4) yields, respectively,

(B.9) {∂tζ+∇⋅(h​𝐮)=0,∂tψ+ζ+ϵ2​|𝐮|2=μ​ϵ​(ℛ⁡[h,𝐮]+ℛb​[h,β​b,𝐮]),\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta+\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u})=0,\\ \\ \partial_{t}\psi+\zeta+\frac{\epsilon}{2}\lvert{\bf u}\rvert^{2}=\mu\epsilon\big(\mathcal{R}[h,{\bf u}]+\mathcal{R}_{b}[h,\beta b,{\bf u}]\big),\end{array}\right.

and

(B.10) {∂tζ+∇⋅(h​𝐮)=0,(∂t+ϵ𝐮⟂curl)𝐯+∇ζ+ϵ2∇(|𝐮|2)=μϵ∇(ℛ[h,𝐮]+ℛb[h,βb,𝐮]),\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta+\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u})=0,\\ \\ \big(\partial_{t}+\epsilon{\bf u}^{\perp}\curl\big)\mathbf{v}+\nabla\zeta+\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla(\lvert{\bf u}\rvert^{2})=\mu\epsilon\nabla\big(\mathcal{R}[h,{\bf u}]+\mathcal{R}_{b}[h,\beta b,{\bf u}]\big),\end{array}\right.

where 𝐯=∇ψ\mathbf{v}=\nabla\psi, 𝐮=def𝔗[h,βb]−1(h∇ψ){\bf u}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}(h\nabla\psi), curl⁡(v1,v2)=def∂1v2−∂2v1\curl(v_{1},v_{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\partial_{1}v_{2}-\partial_{2}v_{1}, (u1,u2)⟂=def(−u2,u1)(u_{1},u_{2})^{\perp}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}(-u_{2},u_{1}), and

ℛ⁡[h,𝐮]\displaystyle\mathcal{R}[h,{\bf u}] =def𝐮3​h⋅∇(h3∇⋅𝐮)+12h2(∇⋅𝐮)2,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{{\bf u}}{3h}\cdot\nabla(h^{3}\nabla\cdot{\bf u})+\frac{1}{2}h^{2}(\nabla\cdot{\bf u})^{2},
ℛb​[h,β​b,𝐮]\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{b}[h,\beta b,{\bf u}] =def−12(𝐮h⋅∇(h2(β∇b⋅𝐮))+h(β∇b⋅𝐮)∇⋅𝐮+(β∇b⋅𝐮)2).\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}-\ \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{{\bf u}}{h}\cdot\nabla\big(h^{2}(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u})\big)+h(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u})\nabla\cdot{\bf u}+(\beta\nabla b\cdot{\bf u})^{2}\right).

System (B.10) is the system we study, and we show in Proposition 6.1 that it is equivalent to the standard formulation of the Green-Naghdi system, namely (1.1). System (B.9) is immediately deduced in the situation curl⁡𝐯=0\curl\mathbf{v}=0, and inherit the canonical Hamiltonian structure of the Zakharov/Craig-Sulem formulation of the water waves system. Notice that one can rewrite system (B.10) as

(B.11) {∂tζ+∇⋅(h​𝐮)=0,(∂t+ϵ𝐮⟂curl)𝐯+∇(ζ+ϵ𝐮⋅𝐯−ϵ2𝐮⋅𝐮−ϵ​μ2w2)=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta+\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u})=0,\\ \\ \big(\partial_{t}+\epsilon{\bf u}^{\perp}\curl\big)\mathbf{v}+\nabla\left(\zeta+\epsilon{\bf u}\cdot\mathbf{v}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}{\bf u}\cdot{\bf u}-\frac{\epsilon\mu}{2}w^{2}\right)=0,\end{array}\right.

with w=(β∇b)⋅𝐮−h∇⋅𝐮w=(\beta\nabla b)\cdot{\bf u}-h\nabla\cdot{\bf u}. To our knowledge, system (B.11), as a new formulation for the Green-Naghdi system, has been first brought to light in [12, (4.3)-(4.4)] (in the flat bottom case, the formulation (B.9) appears in [39, (6.5)] and [46, (9.12)] but is quickly disregarded in favor of the aforementioned ill-posed model). It appears also in [30, (5.14)-(5.15)] (in the irrotational setting), [22, (30)] (in the flat bottom situation) and [38, (2.9)-(2.34)-(2.35)]. As a matter of fact, the latter references point out that system (B.11) echoes a formulation of the water waves system. Indeed, system (B.4) may be equivalently written as

(B.12) {∂tζ+∇⋅(h​𝐮)=0,(∂t+ϵU⟂curl)𝐯+∇(ζ+ϵU⋅𝐯−ϵ2U⋅U−ϵ​μ2w2)=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}\zeta+\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u})=0,\\ \\ \big(\partial_{t}+\epsilon U^{\perp}\curl\big)\mathbf{v}+\nabla\left(\zeta+\epsilon U\cdot\mathbf{v}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}U\cdot U-\frac{\epsilon\mu}{2}w^{2}\right)=0,\end{array}\right.

where 𝐯,U,w\mathbf{v},U,w are determined from the velocity potential, ϕ\phi, by

𝐯=∇(ϕ|)z=1+ϵ​ζ,𝐮=∫β​b1+ϵ​ζ∇ϕdz,U=(∇Xϕ)|,z=1+ϵ​ζw=1μ(∂zϕ)|.z=1+ϵ​ζ\mathbf{v}=\nabla\big(\phi\left|{}_{{}_{z=1+\epsilon\zeta}}\right.\big),\quad{\bf u}=\int_{\beta b}^{1+\epsilon\zeta}\nabla\phi\ {\rm d}z,\quad U=(\nabla_{X}\phi)\left|{}_{{}_{z=1+\epsilon\zeta}}\right.,\quad w=\frac{1}{\mu}(\partial_{z}\phi)\left|{}_{{}_{z=1+\epsilon\zeta}}\right..

System (B.12) is determined by the sole variables ζ\zeta and 𝐯\mathbf{v} (and bb), after solving the Laplace problem (B.2). Now, by the identity (B.5) and chain rule, one has

U=𝐯−μϵw∇ζ and w=ϵU⋅∇ζ−∇⋅(h𝐮).U=\mathbf{v}-\mu\epsilon w\nabla\zeta\quad\text{ and }\quad w=\epsilon U\cdot\nabla\zeta-\nabla\cdot(h{\bf u}).

It follows in particular

U=𝐯+𝒪(μ)=𝐮+𝒪(μ) and w=(β∇b)⋅𝐮−h∇⋅𝐮+𝒪(μ),U=\mathbf{v}+\mathcal{O}(\mu)={\bf u}+\mathcal{O}(\mu)\quad\text{ and }\quad w=(\beta\nabla b)\cdot{\bf u}-h\nabla\cdot{\bf u}+\mathcal{O}(\mu),

and therefore (B.11) is immediately seen as a 𝒪⁡(μ2)\mathcal{O}(\mu^{2}) approximation of (B.12), with the abuse of notation 𝐮=def𝔗​[h,β​b]−1​(h​𝐯){\bf u}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\mathfrak{T}[h,\beta b]^{-1}(h\mathbf{v}) and w=def(β∇b)⋅𝐮−h∇⋅𝐮w\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}(\beta\nabla b)\cdot{\bf u}-h\nabla\cdot{\bf u} being justified by the above approximations.
